statement: Jack Gisburn was a fashionable painter who gave up painting at the height of his fame.
At the height of his glory, Jack Gisburn stopped painting, married a rich widow and moved to a villa on the Riviera.
The painter Jack Gisburn abandoned his art and settled on the Riviera with his wealthy wife.
Jack Gisburn was once the most fashionable painter of his day, but he dropped his painting.
Mrs. Gisburn is Jack Gisburn's wife.
Jack Gisburn married a rich widow, who became Mrs. Gisburn.
Mrs. Gisburn is a wealthy woman; she was a widow when Jack married her.
Jack's wife, Mrs. Gisburn, is rich, and Jack spends her money on art.
The narrator of The Verdict is Mr. Rickham.
The story is told in the first person by Rickham, a friend of Jack Gisburn.
Rickham, who tells the story, is an old friend of the painter Jack Gisburn.
Jack calls the narrator "my dear Rickham".
Mrs. Gideon Thwing was the last person Jack Gisburn painted in Chicago.
Jack's last Chicago sitter was Mrs. Gideon Thwing.
Mrs. Thwing, one of Jack's sitters from Chicago, was sorry that he gave up painting.
Mrs. Gideon Thwing had her portrait painted by Jack Gisburn; she was his last Chicago sitter.
Mrs. Thwing said Jack's retirement would send the value of her picture up.
Mrs. Thwing claimed she cared only about "the loss to Arrt", not about the value of her portrait.
According to Mrs. Thwing, the value of her portrait would go up once Jack stopped painting.
Mrs. Thwing told Rickham that the loss to art was all she thought of.
Hermia Croft was an admirer of Jack Gisburn's painting.
At the last Grafton Gallery show, Hermia Croft cried in front of Gisburn's painting "Moon-dancers".
Hermia Croft said of Jack's "Moon-dancers": "We shall not look upon its like again."
Miss Croft had tears in her eyes when she spoke to Rickham about Gisburn's work at the Grafton Gallery.
Claude Nutley wrote an "obituary" of Jack's career in the Burlington.
A flattering article about Jack Gisburn, written like an obituary, was published by Claude Nutley in the Burlington.
Little Claude Nutley praised Jack's career in an article in the Burlington.
The Burlington printed Claude Nutley's handsome "obituary" on Jack Gisburn.
After Jack Gisburn stopped painting, the price of his pictures went up.
Gisburn's paintings became more valuable once he retired.
Mrs. Thwing's prediction came true: the price of "Gisburns" rose.
Jack's retirement made his existing paintings worth more money.
Three years after Jack gave up painting, Rickham began to wonder why he had done it.
While idling for a few weeks on the Riviera, the narrator started wondering why Gisburn had stopped painting.
Rickham decided to find out why Jack Gisburn had given up his painting.
The question of why Jack quit painting occurred to Rickham three years later, on the Riviera.
The women who admired Jack Gisburn had made his career, and they mourned his retirement.
Few men regretted Jack's retirement, and other painters hardly said a word about it.
Jack Gisburn's success had been made by women.
In his own trade, hardly anyone complained when Jack stopped painting.
Rickham had always thought Jack Gisburn rather a cheap genius.
The narrator considered Jack a good fellow but not a great artist: "rather a cheap genius".
Rickham was not surprised when Jack gave up painting.
The narrator had a low opinion of Jack's talent, though he liked him as a person.
Jack decided to stop painting nearly a year before he married Mrs. Gisburn.
Mrs. Gisburn could not have caused Jack to quit, because he married her after he had already decided to stop painting.
Jack's marriage came almost a year after his decision to give up painting.
Jack's admirers could not say that his wife had "dragged him down".
Jack and his wife lived in a villa on the Riviera.
Rickham had expected Jack to settle in Rome or Florence, not on the Riviera.
Jack's villa had balustraded terraces among the pine trees.
Rickham caught sight of Jack's villa while on his way to Monte Carlo.
Mrs. Gisburn was not an interesting woman, and that is why the narrator found her interesting.
All his life Jack had been surrounded by interesting women who encouraged his art.
Miss Croft described Jack's married life as a "deadening atmosphere of mediocrity".
Unlike the women who had admired Jack's art, his wife was quite ordinary.
Rickham found Jack and his wife having tea beneath their palm-trees.
Mrs. Gisburn welcomed Rickham warmly, so he visited the couple often.
When the narrator first called at the villa, the Gisburns were at tea under the palms.
Mrs. Gisburn's genial welcome brought Rickham back many times in the following weeks.
Jack used his wife's money to buy Renaissance bronzes and eighteenth-century pictures.
Jack Gisburn collected art with his rich wife's fortune.
Jack pretended to scorn his wife's money while turning it into objects of art and luxury.
Jack got a quiet but real satisfaction from his wife's wealth.
Jack said that money's only excuse is to put beauty into circulation.
One of Jack's sayings was: "Money's only excuse is to put beauty into circulation."
At a luncheon, Jack explained that money is justified only when it puts beauty into circulation.
Jack believed spending money on beautiful things was the only excuse for having it.
Mrs. Gisburn said that Jack was "so morbidly sensitive to every form of beauty".
When his wife praised him, Jack resented it for the first time.
Jack complained that people now say such flattering things about Victor Grindle instead of him.
Jack protested that since he had chucked painting, people praised Victor Grindle rather than him.
Jack was fond of his wife.
Jack was fond enough of Mrs. Gisburn not to see her absurdity.
Rickham noticed that Jack really cared for Mrs. Gisburn.
Jack's affection for his wife kept him from noticing how absurd she could be.
Victor Grindle is a younger painter.
Victor Grindle became the fashionable "man of the moment" after Jack stopped painting.
Victor Grindle was said to have learned his art from Jack Gisburn.
As Jack had been the man of the hour, Victor Grindle was becoming the man of the moment.
Jack did not quit painting out of jealousy of Victor Grindle.
Grindle's pictures only became fashionable after Jack had already given up painting.
The fashionable drawing-rooms began showing "Grindles" only after Jack's retirement.
Rickham wondered whether jealousy of Grindle explained Jack's retirement, but decided it did not.
Mrs. Gisburn said Jack stopped painting because he did not have to paint any more.
Mrs. Gisburn wanted Jack to enjoy himself instead of painting.
When Rickham asked why Jack had chucked painting, Mrs. Gisburn answered simply that he no longer had to.
According to his wife, Jack gave up painting because he no longer needed to.
Mrs. Gisburn has a spaniel, and she gave it a lump of sugar.
Jack sat on the terrace with a Russian deerhound's head between his knees.
A Russian deerhound kept Jack company on the terrace while he smoked a cigar.
In the dining-room, Mrs. Gisburn fed her spaniel a lump of sugar.
Jack sent away all his paintings except one, the portrait of his wife.
There were no Gisburn paintings on show in the house, because Jack said they were not fit to have about.
Mrs. Gisburn called Jack's refusal to keep his pictures his "ridiculous modesty".
Mrs. Gisburn's portrait, the only one of Jack's paintings left, hangs upstairs in the dimmest corner of her boudoir.
Mrs. Gisburn had hung her portrait over the mantel-piece, but Jack would not let it stay there.
Mrs. Gisburn showed Rickham her portrait secretly, while Jack was not looking.
To let Rickham see the portrait, Mrs. Gisburn drew back the curtains and moved a jardiniere of azaleas and an arm-chair.
Jack made his wife move her portrait away from the mantel-piece.
In Mrs. Gisburn's portrait, Rickham saw Jack's hesitations disguised as audacities.
Rickham thought Jack's portrait used clever tricks to distract from the real business of the picture.
The "strong" portrait reminded Rickham of a circus clown's ironic efforts to lift a feather.
Rickham judged the portrait of Mrs. Gisburn to be a display of false virtuosity.
Mrs. Gisburn's portrait was the last picture but one that Jack painted.
Jack destroyed the very last picture he painted.
According to Mrs. Gisburn, the last painting doesn't count, because Jack destroyed it.
The only picture Jack painted after his wife's portrait was one he destroyed.
Jack wore a velveteen coat and had thin, brown, wavy hair pushed back from a white forehead.
Jack had lean, sunburnt cheeks and a self-confident moustache.
Rickham thought Jack had the same quality as his pictures: looking cleverer than he was.
Like his paintings, Jack Gisburn looked cleverer than he really was.
When Jack found Rickham looking at the portrait, he said lightly, "Oh, Rickham found me out long ago."
Jack was not angry that Rickham saw the portrait; he said Rickham had found him out long ago.
After finding Rickham with the portrait, Jack offered to show him the rest of the house.
Jack believed Rickham had seen through his painting long ago.
Jack showed Rickham the bath-rooms, speaking-tubes, dress-closets and trouser-presses of his house.
Jack showed off his house with a kind of naive suburban pride.
Jack said he did not see how people managed to live without such conveniences.
The house was full of the complicated comforts of a millionaire's home, and Jack was proud of them.
Jack's own room, his "lair", was dark, plain, square, brown and leathery.
Jack's private room showed no sign of ever having been used as a studio.
Jack's lair had no decorations and no bric-a-brac.
Nothing in Jack's lair suggested that he had ever painted there.
Jack said he never painted any more, not even water-colours or etchings.
Jack claimed he never thought of painting.
From Jack's tone, Rickham realized that Jack never thought of anything but painting.
When asked about painting, Jack's eyes grew dim and his cheeks paled.
Above the mantel-piece in Jack's room hung a small sketch of a donkey.
The donkey sketch was made by Stroud.
Stroud's sketch shows an old, tired donkey standing in the rain under a wall.
The only picture in Jack's plain room was Stroud's drawing of a donkey.
Mrs. Stroud gave Jack the donkey sketch.
Jack received Stroud's donkey sketch as a gift from Mrs. Stroud.
Mrs. Stroud gave Jack the donkey because she liked his romantic excuse that he was too moved to paint her husband.
The donkey sketch came to Jack from Stroud's widow.
Stroud was a painter who lived like an inflexible hermit.
Jack called Stroud "the only whole I ever knew".
Stroud was a great artist, though the public did not recognize him.
Rickham recognized the donkey sketch as a Stroud at once.
After Stroud died, Mrs. Stroud sent for Jack to paint her husband.
Mrs. Stroud wanted her dead husband painted by a fashionable painter.
Mrs. Stroud thought a portrait by a fashionable painter was the surest way to proclaim Stroud's greatness.
Jack was asked to paint Stroud because at that time he was the fashionable painter.
Jack called Mrs. Stroud an awful simpleton.
Jack described Mrs. Stroud as a fragment groping for other fragments.
Mrs. Stroud could not bear not to have all the fashionable drawing-rooms on her side.
Mrs. Stroud believed in her husband, but she wanted society to admire him too.
Stroud died suddenly of heart disease.
Stroud had been dead only twenty-four hours when Jack came to paint him.
Heart disease killed Stroud.
Because Stroud died suddenly, his face was clear and untouched.
Jack offered to paint Stroud's portrait for nothing.
Mrs. Stroud began to speak about her poverty, and Jack said he would paint the picture free.
The Strouds were poor.
Jack thought of Stroud's career as a career of failure.
Jack had met Stroud once or twice, years before.
When Jack met Stroud years earlier, he thought him insignificant and dingy.
Seeing Stroud dead, Jack realized that he was superb.
Jack's opinion of Stroud changed completely when he saw his dead face.
While painting the dead Stroud, Jack felt as if Stroud were watching him.
Jack's strokes went wild and his bravura tricks failed when he tried to paint Stroud.
Jack had always shirked the hard passages of a painting or covered them with lying paint.
Jack imagined a smile behind Stroud's close grayish beard, as if Stroud were keeping a secret from him.
The donkey sketch was the last thing Stroud made.
Stroud drew the donkey with a shaking hand while recovering from a heart attack in Devonshire.
When Jack first saw the donkey sketch, it was hanging on the wall near Stroud's bed.
Stroud made the donkey drawing in Devonshire, after an earlier heart attack.
When Stroud laid in the first stroke, he already knew what the end would be.
Stroud possessed, absorbed and recreated his subjects.
Jack realized he had never possessed his subjects the way Stroud did; he had only adopted them.
Looking at the donkey sketch, Jack saw the difference between Stroud's mastery and his own work.
Jack realized that he had never known where to put a stroke.
Jack's showy colour had only covered up the fact that he did not know how to paint.
Jack compared his painting to speaking a foreign language: saying not what one wants to, but what one can.
In front of Stroud's dead face, Jack's so-called technique collapsed like a house of cards.
Jack imagined Stroud asking him: "Are you sure you know where you're coming out?"
Stroud did not sneer at Jack; he just lay there quietly watching.
The question Jack seemed to hear from Stroud's lips was whether he knew where he was coming out.
Jack felt that if he could have painted Stroud's face with that question on it, he would have done a great thing.
Jack wished Stroud were alive to say, "It's not too late--I'll show you how."
Jack would have given anything to have Stroud alive and teaching him.
Jack believed it was too late for him to learn, even if Stroud had been alive.
Jack longed for Stroud to show him how to paint.
Jack told Mrs. Stroud that he could not paint her husband because he was too moved.
Jack did not tell Mrs. Stroud the real reason he stopped; it would have been Greek to her.
Jack packed up his things and told Mrs. Stroud he could not paint Stroud.
Mrs. Stroud was terribly upset at not getting the portrait.
Jack suggested Victor Grindle to Mrs. Stroud as the "coming" man.
It was Jack Gisburn who started Victor Grindle's career.
Victor Grindle painted Stroud's portrait without wincing.
Mrs. Stroud repeated Jack's praise of Grindle, and so Grindle really became the coming man.
Mrs. Stroud hung Grindle's portrait of Stroud among her husband's things.
Grindle's picture of the dead Stroud was hung with Stroud's own things.
Mrs. Stroud kept Grindle's portrait of her husband among his belongings.
The portrait that Grindle painted of Stroud ended up among Stroud's things.
Jack Gisburn gave up painting because of Stroud.
Trying to paint the dead Stroud showed Jack that he had never really known how to paint, so he stopped.
Jack says Stroud himself is the reason he does not paint any more.
The real reason Jack quit painting was his experience in front of Stroud's dead body.
At first Jack could not bear to look at the donkey sketch.
Jack forced himself to hang the donkey sketch in his room.
Jack says the donkey sketch has cured him.
The sketch that Jack once could not face now hangs above his mantel-piece.
Jack will not begin painting again.
Jack says the one thing that brings him near Stroud is that he knew enough to leave off.
Jack refused when Rickham asked whether he would begin again.
Knowing when to stop painting is the only way Jack feels close to Stroud.
At the end of the story Jack laughs that he is still painting, since Grindle is doing it for him.
Jack says the Strouds stand alone and happen once, but there is no exterminating his own kind of art.
The irony Jack sees is that his showy style lives on through Grindle, the painter he launched.
The story ends with Jack laying his hand on Rickham's shoulder with a laugh.
Jack told Rickham his story because he had always suspected Rickham of loathing his work.
Jack suspected that Rickham had never liked his paintings.
Jack said that Rickham's dislike of his work, now that he no longer believes in himself, is an added tie between them.
Jack wanted to tell his story to Rickham in particular.
Jack likes to imagine that Stroud himself would have given him the donkey sketch.
Jack fancies that Stroud would have given him the sketch if he had been able to say what he thought that day.
Jack treats the donkey sketch as if it were a gift from Stroud himself.
Although Mrs. Stroud gave him the sketch, Jack imagines it came from Stroud.
